summary: A list of assigned IP network numbers and EGP autonomous system numbers. It replaces RFC 997 and was itself replaced by RFC 1062, RFC 1117 and RFC 1166.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a record of which networks have which numbers, like an address book that had to be reissued as the Internet grew.

subtitle: The official record of assigned IP networks and autonomous system numbers.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew beyond the early research labs, administering network numbers and autonomous system assignments became too much for individuals to manage, requiring a formal, centralized registry.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1020 documents all assigned network numbers (in IP Classes A, B, C, and D) and autonomous system numbers as of November 1987. It expands on previous registries by including detailed contact information for network administrators and clarifying the assignment process through the Hostmaster.
tldr.outcome: Rapid growth and fragmentation soon made centralized registries obsolete. Modern Internet number allocation is distributed to Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) responsible for different geographic regions, with IANA maintaining the master allocations.

today: RFC 1020 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1062, RFC 1117, and RFC 1166. Modern network number and autonomous system assignment is managed by IANA and Regional Internet Registries, which distribute assignments across geographic regions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1020 is an official status report on network numbers and autonomous system numbers used in the Internet community as of November 1987. Unlike the earlier RFC 943, responsibility for number assignments has shifted from individual researchers to the Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI International, with Dr. Jon Postel and Joyce Reynolds providing ongoing assistance.

The RFC updates and supersedes RFC 997 and earlier registries. It documents all currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems, along with the name and network mailbox of the responsible individual for each registered network or autonomous system. The document notes that information changes continuously and can be obtained directly from the Hostmaster.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like RFC 943, but three years later and with an even bigger list. By now, assigning numbers had become a whole job at one organization, not just something a person did on the side.

sections.title: Expanded Address Classes and Notation
sections.content:
RFC 1020 documents the same three primary address classes as RFC 943 (Classes A, B, and C), but adds clearer coverage of Class D addresses (used for multicast) and Class E addresses (reserved for future use). Class A networks have a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address (128 possible networks). Class B networks have a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address (16,384 possible networks). Class C networks have a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address (2,097,152 possible networks).

The RFC uses dotted decimal notation: Class A networks are written as nnn.rrr.rrr.rrr, Class B as nnn.nnn.rrr.rrr, and Class C as nnn.nnn.nnn.rrr. The document emphasizes that the Internet Protocol uses 32-bit addresses and explains big-endian transmission order of octets.
sections.plainLanguage: This explains the four types of addresses: big ones (A), medium ones (B), small ones (C), and special ones for groups (D) and future use (E).

sections.title: Network Categories and Assignments
sections.content:
Networks are assigned to four categories marked with a letter: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-Defense), and C for Commercial. The RFC lists assigned network numbers for all three address classes, noting that some networks are permanent and some are independent (marked with an asterisk).

The document also lists autonomous system numbers (ASNs), which identify networks in border gateway routing. Each network assignment includes the responsible party's contact information. The RFC notes that assignments change over time as networks are added, removed, or renumbered.
sections.plainLanguage: Different types of organizations (research, military, government, business) got different blocks of network numbers. Each entry says who was in charge of that network.

sections.title: The Hostmaster and Centralized Assignment
sections.content:
RFC 1020 marks a significant shift: assignment authority is now centralized at the Hostmaster's office within the DDN Network Information Center at SRI. Organizations needing new network numbers or autonomous system numbers must contact the Hostmaster, and the Hostmaster maintains the authoritative registry.

The RFC provides clear contact information: the Hostmaster office accepts phone calls, email, and formal mail requests. The document notes that people sometimes change electronic mailboxes, so the NIC WHOIS service (NICNAME) can be used to find the latest contact information for any registered network administrator.
sections.plainLanguage: Unlike the old system where one researcher assigned numbers, there is now a whole office (the Hostmaster) responsible for keeping track and handing out new network numbers.

sections.title: Obsolescence and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 1020 is now historic, having been superseded by RFC 1062, RFC 1117, and RFC 1166. Even as RFC 1020 was published, the Internet's rapid growth was making centralized registries like this difficult to maintain. Networks were being added constantly, and the registries quickly became outdated.

Today, Internet number allocation is handled by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) and five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) covering different geographic regions: AFNIC (Africa), APNIC (Asia-Pacific), LACNIC (Latin America and the Caribbean), RIPENCC (Europe and the Middle East), and ARIN (North America and parts of the Atlantic).
sections.plainLanguage: This document is now historic. The Internet grew so fast that one office couldn't keep up, so the job got split among several regional organizations around the world.
